issues.legal_issue: A religious head’s beneficial interest in endowed property is a proprietary interest protected by the constitutional right to hold property, and restrictions that substantially impair that interest or the head’s institutional role are invalid.
material_facts: The religious head held office as the spiritual superior of a religious institution and had a beneficial interest in its endowments, together with substantial powers of administration and disposal.

The law subjected surplus-fund expenditure to official directions or permission, restricted the use and accounting of personal gifts, and permitted an official to require or make the appointment of a manager without a prerequisite of mismanagement.
The appeal challenged the constitutional validity of those controls.
issues.conclusion: Sections 30(2), 31 and 55 were invalid as unreasonable restrictions on the religious head’s property rights; section 56 was invalid because it could deprive the head of administration of the trust property and impair the right protected by Article 26(d).
issues.legal_principle: Article 19(1)(f) protects well-recognized interests bearing the characteristics of proprietary rights. A religious head’s office and beneficial interest are blended and cannot be separated; restrictions may protect the public interest but cannot make the head unfit to perform the office. Article 26(d) protects a denomination’s administration of its property in accordance with law, but a law cannot transfer that administration altogether to another authority. The Court relied on Vidya Varuthi v. Balusami, Monohar v. Bhupendra, Ganesh v. Lal Behary, Bhabatarini v. Ashalata and Angurbala v. Debabrata on the proprietary character of religious offices and interests.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_religious_en: A party challenges the constitutionality of a law regulating a religious institution or its endowments.
predicates.religious_head_has_beneficial_property_i: The head of a religious institution holds office with a beneficial interest in the institution’s property and customary powers of administration or disposal.
predicates.officials_control_surplus_spending: The law makes the head’s use of surplus funds subject to official directions or permission.
predicates.personal_gifts_are_restricted: The law restricts the head’s use of personal gifts or requires accounts for those gifts.
predicates.official_can_take_over_management_withou: The law allows an official to require or make the appointment of a manager without requiring a finding of mismanagement.

issues.definition: When a constitutional challenge concerns a religious head with a beneficial property interest, controls over surplus funds, personal gifts, or management that substantially impair that interest or the head’s role are invalid.

issues.legal_issue: Unrestricted official entry into a religious institution can infringe protected religious practice and the institution’s denominational rights.
material_facts: The law authorized designated officials to enter the premises of a religious institution or place of worship to exercise statutory powers or perform statutory duties.
The entry power was not limited to outer premises and did not require notice or protect worship times, sacred areas, or rites and ceremonies.
issues.conclusion: Section 21 was invalid because its unrestricted entry power interfered with rights protected by Articles 25 and 26.
issues.legal_principle: Articles 25 and 26 protect religious practice as well as belief, subject to the constitutional limits including public order, morality and health. Article 26(b) protects a denomination’s autonomy in deciding which rites and ceremonies are essential to its religion. The Court explained that religious practice is not made secular merely because it involves expenditure, employees or marketable goods; Article 25(2)(a) concerns economic, commercial, political and other secular activities associated with religious practice, not religious practices as such.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_religious_en: A party challenges the constitutionality of a law regulating a religious institution or its endowments.
predicates.officials_may_enter_sacred_areas: The law authorizes public officials to enter religious premises that may include areas reserved for sacred or ritual purposes.
predicates.entry_power_lacks_safeguards_for_rites: The law does not require notice or protect the institution’s sacred areas, worship times, or rites and ceremonies.

issues.definition: If a challenged law permits officials to enter sacred areas without safeguards for religious rites, its unrestricted entry power is invalid.

issues.legal_issue: A religious institution or spiritual fraternity may constitute a religious denomination or a section of one, and the denomination has autonomy over matters of religion while property administration remains subject to law.
material_facts: The institution was one of several religious centres founded by a religious teacher and was associated with followers sharing a common faith and spiritual organization.
The institution was found to be connected with a section of those followers, and its head performed the role of spiritual superior and religious teacher.
issues.conclusion: The institution or spiritual fraternity could qualify as a religious denomination or a section of one; its essential religious practices were protected, while administration of its property could be regulated by law.
issues.legal_principle: Articles 25 and 26 protect religious belief and acts performed in its practice. A denomination is a body with a common faith and organization and a distinctive name, and Article 26(b) protects its autonomy in deciding what rites and ceremonies are essential according to its tenets. Article 26(c) and (d) separately protect the right to acquire and own property and to administer it in accordance with law. The Court also considered Article 25(2)(a) and (b), which permit regulation of secular activities associated with religious practice and laws for social welfare and reform.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_concerns_religi: A constitutional challenge concerns the rights of a religious institution or spiritual fraternity.
predicates.adherents_share_common_faith_and_spiritu: The institution’s adherents share a common faith and an organized spiritual tradition.
predicates.institution_represents_a_distinctive_rel: The institution represents a distinct religious group or a section of such a group.

issues.definition: A religious institution whose adherents share a common faith and spiritual organization and who form a distinct group qualifies for denominational protection.

issues.legal_issue: A law that enables the state to take over administration of a religious institution through notification, while barring access to court to set aside that notification, is invalid.
material_facts: The law provided for notification of religious institutions, after which administration would vest in an executive officer appointed by the government.
The notification provisions did not allow a party to obtain a court order setting aside the notification.
issues.legal_principle: Article 26(d) protects a religious denomination’s right to administer its property in accordance with law. The Court held that the notification provisions were extremely drastic and emphasized that they provided no access to court to set aside an order of notification.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_religious_en: A party challenges the constitutionality of a law regulating a religious institution or its endowments.
predicates.notification_transfers_institutional_adm: The law provides that notification of an institution transfers its administration to a government-appointed executive officer.
predicates.courts_cannot_set_aside_notification: The law does not permit a party to obtain judicial review to set aside the notification.

issues.definition: Where a challenged law transfers a religious institution’s administration to a government appointee upon notification and bars courts from setting the notification aside, the takeover provisions are void.

issues.legal_issue: A compulsory annual contribution is a tax rather than a fee when it is not correlated with the cost of services rendered, and a state legislature cannot impose a tax for which it has no legislative competence.
material_facts: The law required religious institutions to make a compulsory annual contribution calculated by reference to their income.
The collections were not earmarked for the expenses of the services said to be rendered and went to the state’s general fund.
There was no correlation between the amount collected and the expenses incurred by the government in providing the services.
issues.conclusion: Section 76(1) imposed a tax, not a fee, and was void for want of legislative competence in the state legislature.
issues.legal_principle: A tax is a compulsory exaction by public authority for public purposes, enforceable by law, and is not payment for services rendered. A fee is generally a charge for a special benefit or service and must be correlated with the expenses of providing it; the distinction lies primarily between a common burden and payment for a special benefit or privilege. The Court relied on Matthews v. Chicory Marketing Board and Lower Mainland Dairy v. Crystal Dairy Ltd., and referred to Findlay Shirras on the Science of Public Finance. Under the constitutional distribution of legislative powers, the state could legislate concerning fees connected with matters in its legislative field, but this levy was a tax outside its competence.

rule.if: constitutional_challenge_to_compulsory_public_levy and payment_is_compulsory and levy_is_not_correlated_with_service_costs and collections_enter_general_revenue

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_compulsory_p: A party challenges the constitutional validity of a compulsory levy imposed on a class of institutions.
predicates.payment_is_compulsory: The law requires the affected institutions to pay the levy regardless of whether they request the asserted services.
predicates.levy_is_not_correlated_with_service_cost: The amount collected is not tied to the government’s costs of providing the asserted services.
predicates.collections_enter_general_revenue: The collections are not earmarked for the services and instead enter the government’s general revenue.

issues.definition: A compulsory levy uncorrelated with service costs and paid into general revenue is a tax, and where the state lacks competence to impose it the levy is invalid.

issues.legal_issue: A tax supporting secular administration of religious trusts and institutions does not violate the constitutional prohibition on appropriating tax proceeds for the promotion or maintenance of a particular religion.
material_facts: The contribution was imposed to support the proper administration of religious trusts and institutions wherever they existed.
Its purpose was not to foster or preserve Hinduism or any particular religious denomination.
issues.conclusion: The levy did not fall within the prohibition in Article 27, although it was invalid on the separate ground that the state legislature lacked competence to impose it.
issues.legal_principle: Article 27 forbids the specific appropriation of tax proceeds to pay expenses for the promotion or maintenance of a particular religion or religious denomination. The Court reasoned that secular administration of religious trusts and institutions, without favouring a religion or denomination, does not attract that prohibition.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_religious_ad: A party challenges a tax imposed to support the administration of religious trusts or institutions.
predicates.tax_proceeds_support_neutral_administrat: The tax proceeds support administration carried out without favouring a religious group.
predicates.proceeds_do_not_promote_or_maintain_a_pa: The tax proceeds are not specifically used to promote or maintain a particular religion or denomination.

issues.definition: A tax supporting neutral administration of religious institutions without promoting or maintaining a particular religion does not trigger the constitutional religious-funding prohibition.
